mechaber.en:
The law of a dog that took a cake together with a coal, ate the cake, and burned a stack of grain. It contains one seif.
If a dog took a cake and went to the cake owner's stack, placed it there, ate the cake, and the coal attached to it burned the stack, the dog's owner pays full damages for the cake and for the place of the cake, and half-damages for the remainder of the stack. If the dog dragged the cake along the stack, burning it as it went, the owner pays full damages for the cake, half-damages for the place touched by the coal, and is exempt for the rest of the stack. Some say he pays half-damages for the entire stack. This applies where the owner of the coal guarded his fire and closed the door, and the dog dug through and took the cake from the fire. If the owner did not guard his fire, the fire's owner is liable for burning the stack, while the dog's owner is liable for eating the cake and for the place where it lay. Rama: Some say that for the place of the cake each owner pays one half, while for the remainder of the stack the dog's owner pays one quarter and the coal's owner three quarters. If the dog threw the cake onto the stack, the dog's owner pays one quarter even for the place of the cake, and the coal's owner pays three quarters.

a) The language of the Rambam, chapter 2 of Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon, law 17, from the Mishnah on 21a. This cake contains coals, since it was ordinarily baked upon them.
bet) The Gemara's interpretation on 53a.
gimel) An interpretation according to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that liability for fire is because it is like one's arrows, on 22a.
dalet) Rashi explains that it is the dog's force and thus a case of pebbles.
heh) The Raavad objects that pebbles produced through an unusual act should at least incur one quarter damages. The Maggid Mishneh writes that he does not know how to resolve this, but perhaps the Rambam holds that once the vessel was set down, the dog's direct force ended, and it is no longer liable for dragging because the stack burned only through the later dragging. The Kesef Mishneh explains that the Rambam's word for dragging means that the dog flung the coal, as Tosafot explain, and therefore it is exempt. In my humble opinion, the Rambam's wording does not support this, and the Beit Yosef cites the Rashba that all the more so if it flung it, Rabbi Yochanan would impose half damages. The Tur likewise writes this and the Ramah cites it in a gloss.
vav) Ibid., law 18. The Maggid Mishneh writes that this follows the sugya on 23a and the reading before Tosafot. There is another explanation based on the reading, 'let the owner of the coal also be liable,' which is our reading and Rashi's.
zayin) Tosafot likewise write there. The reason is that where there is no partner in liability, the dog owner pays only half, meaning one quarter of the total loss, while the owner of the coal pays three quarters, because whenever full payment cannot be collected from one liable party, it is collected from the other, in accordance with Rav Natan on 33a.

And if it was dragging, etc. See Tosafos there, s.v. "and Rabbi Yochanan," and the Rashba's question. This interpretation fits more naturally because it avoids distinguishing between the place of the coal and the rest of the stack. The Rashba explains, however, that the Gemara means merely that Rabbi Yochanan's view can be established even when it set the coal down, unlike Reish Lakish. This is the meaning of "and some say," etc.; see what I wrote in siman 390 seif 5.
(Collected note) And some say that he pays, etc. The Rosh explains so. He writes that Tosafos did not, though Yam Shel Shlomo says Tosafos spoke only according to Sumchus, since Rabbi Elazar's statement was there established as Sumchus. His words are difficult, for if it were not considered his direct force the liability would be half damages, which itself would answer Rabbi Elazar. Tosafos' question can nevertheless be answered in the manner suggested by Yam Shel Shlomo. (End of note.)
